meta.title: Irish B1 Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1000 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Irish → English (see the Irish, recall the meaning) and English → Irish (see an English meaning, recall the Irish). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1000 words of Irish (Gaeilge) for an intermediate learner, aligned to B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.' — a learner here is able to deal with most situations likely to arise whilst travelling, to produce simple connected text on topics which are familiar or of personal interest, and to describe experiences and events, dreams, hopes and ambitions and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Irish has a graded examination at these levels — the Teastas Eorpach na Gaeilge (TEG) of Maynooth University — whose syllabuses describe each level but do not publish a complete word list, so this deck is not an examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 258 of the 1000 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — work and the economy, society and politics, media and technology, the environment, education, relationships and family life, home and housing, health, travel and experiences, culture and leisure, feelings and opinions, the words of explaining and arguing, the verbs and adjectives of judging, time and frequency, and the connectors that build an argument — and the other 742 are the commonest remaining words of written Irish, counted over the articles of the Irish-language Wikipedia by the WHOLE word: every form of a noun or a verb added together, and every spelling its initial mutations give it (bean, bhean, mbean). No subtitle frequency list exists for Irish, and an encyclopaedia's commonest words lean towards history, places and people, which is why the deck leads with the hand-written vocabulary. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. The 715 nouns carry their gender, which decides how the article changes them (an fear, an bhean), and show the noun with the article, its genitive and its plural (an teach, tí, tithe); the 119 verbs are headed by the imperative, the form Irish dictionaries list a verb by (déan, "do"), and show their present, past, future and verbal noun (déanann, rinne, déanfaidh, déanamh). Behind the All forms fold a verb's tenses go by person, a noun shows its lenited and eclipsed forms (theach, dteach) and a preposition its forms with a pronoun (liom, leat, leis). The spelling is the Official Standard (An Caighdeán Oifigiúil) as Wiktionary gives it. Real example sentences come with 186 of the 1000 words, three apiece for 48 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword; few devices have an Irish voice, so the speaker may be silent. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Irish Wikipedia (ga.wikipedia.org), its articles as of 1 November 2026, counted for this deck (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
